title: A week without my phone
text:
Last month, my editor asked me to try something that seemed impossible: to live for one week without my smartphone. I agreed, although I was secretly worried. Like most people, I check my phone more than a hundred times a day.
The first two days were the hardest. I kept putting my hand in my pocket to look for it, and I felt anxious when I didn't know what was happening in the world. I also had practical problems. I didn't have a map, so I got lost on the way to a meeting, and I had to buy a paper ticket for the train because my ticket was on an app.
By the third day, however, things started to change. On the bus, instead of scrolling through social media, I looked out of the window and noticed buildings I had never seen before, even though I had taken the same route for years. In the evenings, I read two novels, something I hadn't done since university. I also slept better, probably because I wasn't looking at a bright screen just before going to bed.
The biggest surprise was my relationships. Because I couldn't send messages, I had to call my friends from the landline or meet them in person. Our conversations were longer and much more interesting.
When the week ended, I was happy to have my phone back, I have to admit. But I have made some changes. I no longer keep it in my bedroom, and I turn off all notifications except calls. It's a small step, but I feel calmer and more in control of my time.

title: From office to farm
model: Cambridge B1 Preliminary – Reading Part 3 (long text)
text:
For twelve years, Elena Ruiz worked as an accountant in a large company in Madrid. She had a good salary, a nice flat and lots of friends, but she wasn't happy. "Every day was the same," she says. "I spent eight hours looking at numbers on a screen, and then another hour sitting in traffic. I felt that my life was passing me by."
Everything changed during a holiday in Galicia, in the north-west of Spain. Elena stayed on a small farm where the owners produced goat's cheese. She helped them for a few days and loved it. "I was tired at the end of the day, but it was a good kind of tiredness," she explains.
A year later, the farm's owners decided to retire, and they offered to sell it to Elena. Her family thought it was a terrible idea. "My mother cried," she remembers. "She thought I was throwing away my career." But Elena had saved some money, and the bank agreed to lend her the rest.
The first year was very difficult. Two goats became ill, a storm damaged the roof of the barn, and she made very little money. However, she didn't give up. She took an online course in marketing and started selling her cheese on the internet.
Today, five years later, her cheese is sold in shops all over Spain and she employs three people from the village. "I work harder than before, and I earn less," Elena says, "but I wouldn't change my life for anything. And my mother? Now she's my best customer."

title: Lost in Tokyo – and loving it
text:
When I arrived in Tokyo, I had a detailed plan for every day of my trip: temples in the morning, museums in the afternoon, famous restaurants in the evening. By the second day, my plan was in the bin, and that was the best thing that happened to me.
It started when I took the wrong train. Instead of going to the city centre, I ended up in a quiet neighbourhood with narrow streets, tiny houses and flowers in front of every door. There were no tourists at all. I walked around for hours, and I found a small family restaurant where an old man cooked the best noodles I have ever eaten. He didn't speak English and I don't speak Japanese, but we managed to communicate with smiles and gestures. When I left, he gave me a little paper bird as a present.
After that, I decided to travel differently. Every morning, I chose a train line at random and got off at a station I had never heard of. Of course, I still visited some famous places, like the fish market and the big temple in Asakusa, but my best memories are of ordinary places: a public bath, a park where people were practising tai chi, a tiny shop that sold only handmade knives.
My advice? Don't fill every minute of your trip. Leave some time free to get lost. Tokyo is one of the safest cities in the world, the trains are excellent, and you can always find your way back to your hotel. You might discover something that no guidebook will ever tell you about.

title: Should schools start later?
text:
Many teenagers find it very hard to get up in the morning, and their parents often think they are just lazy. However, scientists say that the problem is not laziness but biology.
During adolescence, the body's internal clock changes. Teenagers start to feel sleepy about two hours later than children and adults, often not until eleven o'clock at night or later. At the same time, they need between eight and ten hours of sleep. If school starts at eight, and they have to get up at half past six, it is almost impossible for them to sleep enough.
This lack of sleep has serious effects. Tired students find it more difficult to concentrate and remember information, so their marks can suffer. They are also more likely to feel stressed or depressed, and teenage drivers who haven't slept enough have more accidents.
Some schools have decided to do something about it. In one American city, secondary schools moved their start time from 7:50 to 8:45. After two years, students were sleeping an average of 34 minutes more each night. Their grades improved, and fewer students arrived late or missed classes.
Not everyone agrees with the idea, though. Some parents say that a later start causes problems for families, because they have to leave for work before their children go to school. Others point out that school would finish later too, leaving less time for sports, part-time jobs and homework.
It seems that there is no perfect solution. But perhaps the next time a teenager can't get out of bed, adults should be a little more understanding.

title: The town that stopped using plastic bags
text:
Ten years ago, the small coastal town of Port Ellis had a problem. Every time there was a storm, hundreds of plastic bags blew into the sea. Fishermen found them in their nets, and local people were tired of seeing them on the beach.
It was a group of schoolchildren who decided to act. After a lesson about pollution, a class of eleven-year-olds wrote a letter to every shop in town, asking them to stop giving out plastic bags. They also made a short video showing a turtle that had died after eating one. The video was shared thousands of times online.
At first, some shop owners were not keen. They were afraid that customers would go to the supermarket in the next town instead. But the children didn't stop. They organised a meeting at the town hall, and more than three hundred people came. In the end, all forty-two shops in Port Ellis agreed to the plan.
To help people, local volunteers made cloth bags from old curtains and T-shirts and gave them away for free. The town also put up signs at the entrance to every shop: "Have you got your bag?"
The results were impressive. In the first year, the number of plastic bags found on the beach fell by ninety per cent. Tourists began to visit Port Ellis because they had heard its story, and some shops actually sold more than before.
Today, those schoolchildren are adults. One of them, Mia Carter, now works for an environmental organisation. "We were just kids," she says, "but we learned that ordinary people can change things."

title: The benefits of walking
text:
When people decide to get fit, they often join a gym, buy expensive running shoes or sign up for intense fitness classes. Many of them give up after a few weeks. But according to doctors, one of the best forms of exercise is something almost everyone can do: walking.
Walking for just thirty minutes a day can reduce the risk of heart disease, help control weight and make bones stronger. It is also good for the mind. Studies show that people who walk regularly feel less stressed and sleep better. Some researchers have found that walking, especially in green spaces like parks or forests, can even improve memory and creativity. In fact, several famous writers and scientists used to go for long walks when they needed new ideas.
One of the great advantages of walking is that it is free and doesn't need any special equipment, just a comfortable pair of shoes. You don't need to find time for it in a busy day either. You can walk to work or to the shops instead of driving, take the stairs instead of the lift, or get off the bus one stop early.
To get the most benefits, experts recommend walking fast enough to breathe a little harder than normal, but not so fast that you can't talk. Walking with a friend or a dog can help you keep going, and many people find that using an app to count their steps motivates them.
So next time you think you're too busy or too tired to exercise, just put on your shoes and go out of the door. Your body and your mind will thank you.

title: The history of the sandwich
text:
Every day, millions of people around the world eat a sandwich for lunch. But where does this simple meal come from, and why is it called a 'sandwich'?
According to a popular story, the name comes from John Montagu, the fourth Earl of Sandwich, an English aristocrat who lived in the eighteenth century. The Earl loved playing cards and was said to play for hours without stopping. He didn't want to leave the table to eat a proper meal, so he asked his servant to bring him some meat between two pieces of bread. This way, he could eat with one hand and continue playing with the other, and his fingers didn't get the cards dirty. Soon, his friends began to order "the same as Sandwich", and the name stuck.
However, historians say that this story may not be completely true. Some believe the Earl was actually a hard-working politician who ate at his desk, not at the card table. And of course, he didn't invent the idea. People had been eating bread with other food for thousands of years. In the Middle East, people wrapped meat in flat bread, and in the Middle Ages, Europeans used thick slices of old bread as plates.
What is certain is that the sandwich became extremely popular in England in the nineteenth century, when more people worked in factories and offices and needed a cheap, quick lunch. Today, the British eat around eleven billion sandwiches every year, and the most popular filling is chicken.

title: Ask Anna: my sister borrows everything
model: Cambridge B1 Preliminary – Reading Part 3 (advice column)
text:
Dear Anna,
I'm sixteen and I share a bedroom with my younger sister, Lucy, who is thirteen. We usually get on well, but recently she has started taking my things without asking. She wears my clothes, uses my make-up and last week she even took my headphones to school and lost them. I bought those headphones with money from my summer job, so I was really upset. When I complain to my parents, they just say, "She's your sister, you should share." I feel like nobody understands me. What can I do?
Jessica

Dear Jessica,
First of all, your feelings are completely normal. It's hard when you don't have your own space, and it's even harder when someone doesn't respect your belongings.
I suggest that you talk to Lucy calmly, at a time when you are not angry. Explain how you felt when she lost your headphones. She might not realise how much they meant to you. Then try to agree on some rules together. For example, she can borrow certain clothes if she asks first, but your make-up and electronic things are off-limits.
It's also a good idea to talk to your parents again, but this time, don't complain. Instead, ask for practical help. Perhaps they could buy you a small box with a lock for your most important things, or divide the wardrobe so that each of you has your own side.
Finally, remember that Lucy probably borrows your things because she admires you. That doesn't make it right, but it might help you be a little more patient.
Anna

title: The climber who started at sixty
text:
Most people think that rock climbing is a sport for young, strong people. Margaret Hill disagrees. She climbed her first wall at the age of sixty, and now, at seventy-three, she goes climbing three times a week.
"It all started because of my grandson," Margaret explains. "He had a birthday party at a climbing centre, and while the children were climbing, the instructor asked if I wanted to try. I laughed and said I was far too old. But he insisted, so I put on a harness and went up a few metres. I was terrified, but when I came down, I felt fantastic."
The next week, Margaret signed up for a beginners' course. She admits that it wasn't easy. "My arms were weak and I had no idea how to use my feet properly. The other students were in their twenties, and I was always the slowest." But she kept going, and slowly her strength and technique improved.
Today, Margaret climbs outdoors as well as indoors. Last summer, she and a group of friends from the climbing centre spent two weeks climbing in the mountains of northern Italy. She has also started a club for people over fifty, which now has more than forty members.
According to Margaret, climbing has given her much more than physical fitness. "You have to concentrate completely, so you forget all your worries. And you have to trust the person holding your rope, so you make real friends." Her advice for older people who want to try something new is simple: "Don't listen to the voice that says you can't. Just try it."

title: How to save money as a student
text:
Going to university is an exciting time, but for many students it is also the first time they have to manage their own money. Rent, books, food and going out can be very expensive, and it's easy to run out of money before the end of the month. Here are some tips from students who have learned the hard way.
The most important thing is to make a budget. At the start of each month, write down how much money you have and what you need to pay for. Then decide how much you can spend each week on food and fun. Several free apps can help you keep track of your spending.
Food is often the biggest expense after rent. Instead of buying lunch every day, which can cost more than a hundred euros a month, cook at home and take your lunch with you. Cooking with your flatmates is cheaper and more fun than cooking alone, and buying large packets of rice or pasta together saves even more.
Don't buy all your books new. Look for second-hand copies online, ask older students if they want to sell theirs, or use the university library. Many students also forget to ask for student discounts. Cinemas, museums, clothes shops and even some restaurants offer them, so always carry your student card.
Finally, think carefully before you get a credit card. It can be useful in an emergency, but it's very easy to spend money you don't have. As one student said: "The worst part about debt is that it follows you long after you have finished studying."
